Case-insensitive counts over the whole text: 'externally managed' 0, 'external manager' 0, 'Vermoegensverwalt' 0, 'Mandat' 0, 'ETF' 0, 'Investmentfonds' 0, 'World Bank' 0, 'Weltbank' 0, 'RAMP' 0, 'Crown Agents' 0, 'BlackRock' 0, 'Amundi' 0, 'PIMCO' 0. The PDF at publikationen.bundesbank.de/publikationen-de/content/951398/download 404s; the /content/951398 HTML edition is the working route and contains the same text.

HM Treasury, 'Exchange Equalisation Account: Annual Report and Accounts 2024-25' (https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6939959e7a605b2d61cd909b/EEA_Annual_Report_and_Accounts_2024-25.pdf), downloaded and read in full (144,041 characters). This is the document where UK official reserves management is reported, the reserves sitting in the EEA rather than on the Bank of England's own balance sheet. It states management is in house and names no outside manager: 'HM Treasury has appointed the Bank of England (the Bank) to act as its agent in the day-to-day management of the EEA'; 'Overall management of the EEA is the responsibility of HM Treasury which delegates day-to-day management to the Bank, acting as its Agent and Advisor'; and in the Performance Analysis section, under 'Foreign Currency & Gold Reserves', 'Assets in this portfolio are managed by the Bank of England to ensure the EEA is ready to fulfil key reserve management objectives'. The report also records the return from 'the Bank's active management of the reserves' of GBP 49 million in 2024-25 (2023-24: GBP 63 million). Counts over the whole text: 'external manager' 0, 'externally managed' 0, 'external fund' 0, 'investment manager' 0, 'BlackRock' 0, 'Amundi' 0, 'PIMCO' 0, 'Wellington' 0, 'World Bank' 0, 'RAMP' 0, 'Crown Agents' 0; the single 'mandate' hit is the Governor's term of office, not a management mandate. A tie for the Bank of England already exists elsewhere on the map as a party name, so no new party would be needed even if this were filed, but the relation here is the state's own agent, not an outside manager.

Department of Finance Canada, 'Report on the Management of Canada's Official International Reserves, April 1, 2024 - March 31, 2025' (https://www.canada.ca/en/department-finance/services/publications/official-international-reserves/2025.html), opened through WebFetch; canada.ca refused curl three times with 'Empty reply from server' and an HTTP/2 INTERNAL_ERROR, so the PDF at /content/dam/fin/publications/oir-roli/oir-roli-2025-eng.pdf could not be greped and the reading covers characters 0 to 100,000 of the page's 147,694 (the funding and investment policy, the EFA portfolio composition and the governance sections; the last third, mostly statistical tables, was not read). Canada's reserves sit in the Exchange Fund Account rather than on the Bank of Canada's balance sheet, and this is the report that would name any outside manager. It names only state bodies: 'The Department of Finance Canada and the Bank of Canada jointly develop and implement the funding and investment policy' of the EFA; the Bank of Canada, as fiscal agent, 'executes funding and investment transactions and manages EFA cash flows'; and the Funds Management Committee of senior officials from both bodies 'oversees the management of the EFA'. The Bank for International Settlements appears only as a place cash is deposited ('Cash deposits with central banks and the Bank for International Settlements'), not as a manager. No mention of an external manager, externally managed assets, an investment manager, outsourcing, the World Bank, or any named private asset-management firm.

Banque de France, Annual Report 2024, chapter 7 'Financial management and accounts' (https://www.banque-france.fr/system/files/2025-05/financial_management_and_accounts_Report_annual_2024_.pdf), downloaded and read in full (113,823 characters), containing the balance sheet, the profit and loss account, the accounting policies and all 24 notes, including asset item A2 'foreign currency denominated securities held in connection with foreign exchange reserve management' and the note on the revaluation reserve for state gold and foreign exchange reserves (RRRODE) under the amended state agreement of 3 July 2024. Counts over the whole text: 'gestion deleguee' 0, 'gestionnaires externes' 0, 'gestionnaire externe' 0, 'externally managed' 0, 'OPCVM' 0, 'ETF' 0, 'parts de fonds' 0, 'World Bank' 0, 'Banque mondiale' 0, 'RAMP' 0, 'BlackRock' 0, 'Amundi' 0, 'PIMCO' 0. Two 'mandate' hits, neither a management mandate for the Bank's reserves: Governor Villeroy de Galhau's term as Chair of the BIS Board, and the note on the participating interest in BDF Gestion, which runs the other way round - 'BDF Gestion, the Banque de France's fully-owned asset management subsidiary, manages a wide range of collective investment schemes as well as individual mandates for institutional investors', i.e. the Bank's own subsidiary managing outside institutions' money, not an outside body managing the Bank's reserves. Not filed: the relation on this row is an outside body managing the central bank's reserves, and BDF Gestion is neither outside nor managing them.

Ministry of Finance Singapore, 'Who manages the reserves?' (https://www.mof.gov.sg/policies/reserves/who-manages-the-reserves), read in full - the document r68 named as the next one to open. It states in-house management of the central bank's reserves: 'The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), as the central bank of Singapore, manages the Official Foreign Reserves (OFR) of Singapore.' The page does name an outside fund manager, but for the Government's assets and not for the OFR: 'GIC Private Limited (GIC) is a professional fund manager that manages Government assets', and nowhere does the page say GIC manages the MAS Official Foreign Reserves. Temasek is described as owning its own assets, not as managing Government assets on the Government's behalf. Taken with the r68 reading of the MAS Annual Report 2021/22 'Reserve Management' page, which says the OFR are invested in cash, bonds and equities under an investment universe approved by the MAS Board and names no external fund manager, the row is a documented negative for Singapore. Not filed as a GIC record, because filing GIC against the MAS would be exactly the upgrade the brief forbids - a manager of Government assets is not a manager of the central bank's reserves. Not yet read: the full MAS Annual Report PDF financial statements, which could still carry a figure for externally managed funds.

Banco de Portugal, 'Relatorio do Conselho de Administracao - Atividade e Contas 2024' (https://www.bportugal.pt/sites/default/files/documents/2025-05/relatorio_ca_2024_pt.pdf). bportugal.pt again refused curl, returning 1,002,031 bytes of HTML with a 403 status where the PDF was expected, so the other tool was used as r68 advised: WebFetch rendered the document and three windows were read, characters 0 to 300,000 of 442,081 (the management report and the annual accounts with their notes); the final 142,000 characters were not reached. The document names no external manager - no 'gestores externos', no 'gestao externa', no 'mandatos', no named asset manager, no World Bank or RAMP, and the BIS appears only as a shareholding that paid a EUR 4 million dividend in 2024. What it does carry is a holding of units in outside-managed funds, which the brief says is not mine to decide, so it is reported here and not filed: the Bank says it began investing in exchange-traded fund units - 'O Banco iniciou o investimento em unidades de participacao de exchange-traded funds (ETF)' - to diversify its asset management, and held EUR 60,632 thousand (about EUR 60.6 million) of ETF units at 31 December 2024. The note names neither the funds nor their managers, and gives the figure above. Two further facts that run the other way and are not records on this row: the Bank manages, jointly with the Bank of Lithuania, two ECB reserve portfolios denominated in US dollars and renminbi, worth EUR 1,134 million and EUR 626 million at year-end (the Bank managing the ECB's reserves, not the reverse); and the Bank's pension liabilities are calculated by the Sociedade Gestora dos Fundos de Pensoes do Banco de Portugal, its own in-house pension-fund management company, while public sector deposits held at the Bank are managed by the state treasury agency IGCP - neither is the Bank's own reserves.

Reserve Bank of New Zealand, 'How we manage foreign reserves' (https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/financial-markets/foreign-reserves/how-we-manage-foreign-reserves), read in full. The page refers throughout to 'our reserve managers', which reads as in-house management, but it also carries one sentence that puts part of the portfolio into an outside-managed fund: 'A small portion of the reserves portfolio is currently invested in investment funds managed by the BIS.' Reported as refused and not filed, per the brief's rule that holding units in an outside-managed fund is not mine to decide. On the three questions the brief asks: the note does NOT name the individual fund (it says 'investment funds' in the plural, which would be the BIS investment pools, BISIP, though the page does not use that name), it DOES name the manager - the Bank for International Settlements, which the map already carries under the spelling 'Bank for International Settlements' - and it gives NO figure, only 'a small portion'. If a later round wants to convert this, the document to open is the RBNZ Annual Report 2025 financial statements (https://www.rbnz.govt.nz/hub/publications/corporate-publications/annual-reports/annual-report-2025), which would be where a balance against the BIS funds appears; note that rbnz.govt.nz returned 'Browser issue' placeholders to the search engine for most of its pages, so the PDF route is likelier than the HTML one.

One thin page opened: Ministry of Finance Japan, 'ESG Investment' under the Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account section (https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/international_policy/fefsa/esg_investment.html). It names no manager and no firm, no World Bank, IBRD or BIS, and says only that 'the Ministry of Finance (MOF) has decided to adopt an investment stance' and that it is 'accumulating expertise including through outsourcing' - a phrase that hints at outside help but names nobody and does not say a portfolio is managed, so it fails the brief's no-upgrading rule and is not a record. Japan's foreign reserves are held in the MOF's Foreign Exchange Fund Special Account with the Bank of Japan acting as agent, so the MOF side is where any manager would be named. Next documents: the FEFSA index page at https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/international_policy/fefsa/ and the Japanese-language settlement statements for the Gaikoku Kawase Shikin Tokubetsu Kaikei, grepped for the Japanese for 'entrusted' and 'outsourced' as well as 'external manager'; then the Bank of Japan Annual Review financial statements for the BOJ's own (much smaller) foreign assets.
